title: Who Is Jesus?
subtitle: The one person in two natures, fully God and fully man. Every view the early church considered is stated in its own best voice before the church judged it
triageNote: The identity of Jesus is the center of the faith, fixed at Nicaea and Chalcedon. A different Jesus is a different gospel. This is not a family argument inside the household. This is the door into the house. Get this wrong and everything else, however sincere, is built on someone other than the Christ the apostles knew.
question: When you pray to Jesus, who are you praying to? A great teacher who showed us how to live? An angel or a half-god, the highest creature God ever made? God wearing a human costume that was not really flesh? Or something stranger and harder than any of these, a single person who is at the same time completely God and completely man? He got tired and wept and bled. And He forgave sins, stilled storms, and rose from the dead. The whole faith leans its weight on the answer. Christology is just the long word for asking, with care, exactly who Jesus is.
whyItMatters:
If you are new to faith, you might think this is a puzzle for scholars. That the rest of us can simply love Jesus and leave the definitions to people with more time. I understand the instinct. But hear why the church bled and argued for four centuries to get the words right.

Only a Jesus who is fully God can save you. If He were merely a creature, however exalted, then He could not bear the weight of God's judgment for the sins of the world, and His death would be the death of one good man, no more able to rescue you than the death of any other. Forgiveness on this scale is something only God can give, because the offense is finally against God. So if Jesus is less than God, you are not saved.

And only a Jesus who is fully man can save you. The thing that needed redeeming was human life, lived under the law, tempted, suffering, mortal. If He did not take a real human nature, a real body and a real human mind and will, then He did not stand in your place, because He did not stand where you stand. The old church had a phrase for this, that the unassumed is the unhealed. What Christ did not take up He did not heal. If He skipped any part of being human, that part of you is left outside His rescue.

This is why the identity of Jesus is not a footnote. Salvation itself requires that He be both, truly God and truly man, in one person. The orthodox definition is not the church showing off. It is the church guarding the only Savior who can actually save.

positions.name: Chalcedonian Orthodoxy (the faith of the church)
positions.inOneLine: Jesus is one person who exists in two complete natures, fully God and fully man, the two united in Him without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation.
positions.bestCase:
Begin with the words and let me define them as I go. A nature is the whatness of a thing, the complete set of what it takes to be that kind of being. Human nature is everything it takes to be a man, a body, a soul, a mind, a will. The divine nature is everything it takes to be God, eternal, all-knowing, all-powerful, unchanging. A person is not a what but a who, the someone who has a nature and acts and says I. You have one nature and you are one person. The claim of the church is that Jesus is one person who has two whole natures at once.

We call this the incarnation, from the Latin for becoming flesh, the eternal Son of God taking to Himself a complete human nature without ceasing to be God. The Word, who was God, became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1, John 1:14). He did not turn into a man the way water turns to ice, leaving His divinity behind. He added humanity to His deity. The one who had always been God became also, and forever, man.

The joining of the two natures in the one person is what we name the hypostatic union, from a Greek word for the individual person, the hypostasis. The two natures are united in the single person of the Son. Not two persons sharing an address. One person, the Son, who lives His divine life as God and His human life as man, and it is always the same He doing both. When He stills the storm, that is the Son. When He sleeps in the boat, that is the same Son. One who, two whats.

In the year 451 the church gathered at a town called Chalcedon and set the guardrails with four words that have held ever since. The two natures come together without confusion and without change, meaning they are not blended into a third thing and neither one is turned into the other, so His humanity stays fully human and His deity stays fully divine. And they come together without division and without separation, meaning you may never pull them apart into two Sons or two persons, as if a human Jesus did some things and a divine Christ did others. The four words are fences. Fall off any side and you have lost Him.

Because of this union we can say startling things and mean them precisely. We can say that the one born of Mary is God the Son, and so the church called Mary Theotokos, a Greek title meaning God-bearer, not because she is the source of His divinity, she is not, but because the child in her womb was a single person who was God. We can say that God purchased the church with His own blood (Acts 20:28), because the one whose blood it was is God. This is the faith. One person, two natures, fully God, fully man, the natures unconfused and undivided. Everything else the church rejected was a failure to hold all of that at once.

positions.name: Docetism
positions.inOneLine: Jesus only seemed to be human. His body was an appearance, because the holy God could never truly take on lowly, suffering flesh.
positions.bestCase:
Hear us as we heard ourselves, for we thought we were protecting God's honor. Our name comes from a Greek word meaning to seem. That is our whole claim. The Christ seemed to have a body, seemed to eat, seemed to suffer, but did not truly do these things in the flesh, because flesh is the realm of decay and corruption and God is pure light.

We could not bear the thought that the infinite, untouchable God would soak Himself in blood and bowels and death. To us that was not devotion, it was insult. Surely the divine Christ floated above all that. When He walked, some of us said, He left no footprint. The suffering on the cross was a kind of shadow play, the appearance of agony, not the real wounding of God.

We drew on a wider mood of our age. It treated the material world as a prison and the spirit as the only pure thing. Salvation, we thought, was rescue from the body, not the redemption of it. So a Savior tangled up in a real body made no sense to us. He came to call us out of the flesh, not to wear it.

The church answered us early and hard, while the apostles were barely cold. John wrote that every spirit which does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God (1 John 4:2-3), and Ignatius, carried off to be killed for the faith, insisted Jesus truly was born, truly ate, truly was nailed up, truly died. The church saw the cost of our view at once. If His body was a phantom, then His death was a phantom. And a phantom cannot die for you. If He did not truly take flesh, He did not truly heal flesh, and your body, the thing God means to raise, is left out of salvation. We were ruled outside the faith. A Savior who only seemed human only seems to save.
advocates: Marcion (in his denial of true flesh)

positions.name: Arianism
positions.inOneLine: The Son is the highest and first of all God's creatures, glorious beyond all others, but made, not God in the full sense. There was a time when the Son was not.
positions.bestCase:
We were not crude men, and we were not trying to belittle Christ. We honored Him above everything in heaven and earth. Hear our reasoning on its own terms. God the Father alone is unbegotten, without source, without beginning. That is what it means to be God, to be utterly first. So if the Son is begotten, brought forth from the Father, then He has a source, and what has a source is not the unbegotten God.

From this we drew the line that became our banner, there was once when the Son was not. Before all worlds, yes, before time itself, the Father brought forth the Son as the first and greatest of His works, the one through whom He then made everything else. So the Son is not a creature like you, but He is on the creature side of the line, the firstborn of creation (Colossians 1:15), the beginning of God's creation (Revelation 3:14). We honored Him as the unique Son, more than an angel, less than the Father.

We pointed to His own words. The Father is greater than I (John 14:28). The Son can do nothing of His own accord (John 5:19). He prays, He obeys, He is sent, He grows in wisdom. We asked plainly. Does the most high God obey? Does the most high God not know the day or the hour (Mark 13:32)? To us these were the marks of a being beneath the Father. Exalted but derived.

The church faced us at Nicaea in 325 and refused our line. They confessed the Son to be of one substance with the Father, the very same Godhead, begotten not made, and they planted one word against us that we could not get around. Athanasius spent his life on it. If the Son is a creature, then a creature is our Savior. And no creature can save. Salvation belongs to God alone. Only God can reconcile us to God. And the worship the New Testament gives to Jesus, the prayers offered to Him, the knee that bows to Him, would be idolatry if He were made. The church judged that to make the Son a creature is to lose both true salvation and true worship. So it ruled us out. Begotten not made was the wall they built. It has held.
advocates: later, the homoian and anomoian parties

positions.name: Apollinarianism
positions.inOneLine: In Jesus the divine Word took the place of a human mind. He had a human body and a human soul of the lower kind, but where you have a human rational mind, He had the Word instead.
positions.bestCase:
Follow our concern, for it was a real one. We were fighting the same enemies the church was fighting, and we wanted above all to keep Jesus one. Our worry was this. If Jesus had a complete human nature, a full human mind with its own thoughts and a full human will with its own choices, then He had a human person standing next to the divine person. You have torn Him into two. How do you keep Him one unless something at the center is single?

So we taught that the eternal Word supplied what would otherwise be the human mind. We pictured a man as having a body, a lower animating soul, and a rational mind or spirit at the top. In Jesus, we said, the body and the lower soul were human, but the highest part, the rational governing mind, was the divine Word itself. The Word was the mind of Christ. That kept Him perfectly one. The deepest seat of the self was the Word, and the Word is one.

It also, we thought, kept Him sinless in a clean way. A human mind is where temptation festers and where the will can turn wrong. Put the unchanging Word in that seat and you have a Christ who cannot waver, whose center is pure deity directing a human frame. To us this looked like reverence, a Savior governed at the core by God Himself.

The church, led by men like Gregory of Nazianzus, saw the wound in it and named it with a sentence that decided the matter. That which He has not assumed He has not healed. If the Word did not take a human mind, then the human mind, the very place where our sin runs deepest, was never taken up by Christ. It was never redeemed. You would be saved in your body and lost in your thoughts. Worse, a man without a human mind is not fully a man at all. He is a strange hybrid. The church at Constantinople in 381 ruled us out because a half-taken humanity is a half-finished salvation, and the part He skipped is the part we most need healed.

positions.name: Nestorianism
positions.inOneLine: In Christ there are two persons as well as two natures, a divine Son and a human son, closely joined and working in perfect harmony, but not collapsed into a single who.
positions.bestCase:
Be fair to us, for the church later decided we had been described worse than we deserved, and the real concern under our name is worth hearing. We were horrified by anything that mixed God up with the limits of the man. We wanted to keep the two natures crystal clear and never let the divine be dragged through the human dirt. So we drew the line very sharply. Perhaps too sharply.

Our famous fight was over a single word. The other side wanted to call Mary Theotokos, God-bearer. We recoiled. How can a woman be the mother of God, who has no beginning? She is the mother of the man Jesus. Call her Christotokos, Christ-bearer, the mother of the Christ in His humanity, but do not say that the eternal God was carried in a womb and nursed at a breast. That seemed to us to drown the divine nature in human weakness. It seemed to make God an infant.

So we spoke of the divine Word and the man Jesus as two, joined in a union of will and honor and love so close that they could be addressed as one. The Word dwelt in the man as in a temple. When the man suffered, we would not say God suffered. When the man was born, we would not say God was born. We kept a careful distance at every point where deity and weakness met, because we feared that to join them too tightly was to defile God.

Cyril of Alexandria led the charge against us. The council at Ephesus in 431 ruled us out. The church saw that if there are two persons, then there are two sons, and the one who saves is not the same one who was born and died. The whole power of the gospel is that the one person who is God is the very one who was born of Mary and died on the cross. If a mere human son dies while the divine Son stands apart, then God did not give Himself for us. A man did. The church kept Theotokos precisely to nail down that the child in the manger was a single person who was God. Two natures, yes, always. Two persons, never.
advocates: the Antiochene school in its sharper form

positions.name: Eutychianism (Monophysitism)
positions.inOneLine: After the union the two natures blended into one. The humanity was swallowed up in the deity like a drop of honey in the sea, leaving a single mingled nature that is neither simply God nor simply man.
positions.bestCase:
Hear our zeal. It was zeal for the oneness of Christ and against the splitting we saw in our opponents. We feared the opposite error so much that we ran past the truth. Our name monophysite comes from the Greek for one nature, and that was our cry, one nature after the union.

We reasoned this way. Before the incarnation, yes, there is the divine nature and there will be a human nature. But in the act of becoming flesh the two come together so completely that they fuse into one. Eutyches put it plainly, that he confessed two natures before the union but one nature after it. The humanity is taken so fully into the deity that it is transformed, the way a drop of wine poured into the ocean is still there in some sense but is now ocean, no longer distinct wine.

We thought this honored Christ most highly. It made Him utterly unified. A single divine-human nature so welded that you could never again separate or even distinguish the parts. And it kept His humanity from looking like a second thing alongside His deity. Everything in Him was now drenched in God. To us this was the highest reverence. A Christ wholly one.

The Council of Chalcedon in 451 ruled us out with the very words it chose, that the two natures meet without confusion and without change. The church saw that if the humanity is swallowed up, then He is no longer truly one of us. The drop of honey lost in the sea is no longer honey you can taste. A humanity blended away is a humanity that no longer stands in your place, no longer the real flesh that is tempted, suffers, and dies for you. And a deity altered by mixture is no longer the unchanging God. The church judged that to blend the natures is to lose them both, and so it set the fence, two natures, each kept whole, in one person forever.
advocates: later non-Chalcedonian traditions in disputed and varied forms

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Chalcedonian Orthodoxy (the faith of the church)
biblicalEvidence.summary: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The one who is God from eternity is the very one who took on flesh.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arians seized on the Word being with God to argue the Word is a second, lesser being beside the Father, and some translated the last clause as the Word was a god. Orthodoxy answers that the same verse says the Word was God without qualification. And John 1:14, the Word became flesh, sinks Docetism in a single line. Real flesh, not seeming flesh.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Chalcedonian Orthodoxy (the faith of the church)
biblicalEvidence.summary: Christ, though He was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being born in human likeness. He humbled Himself to death on a cross. Therefore God exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arians read the exaltation as proof the Son was raised to a status He did not have before. A creature promoted. Orthodoxy reads it the other way. Only one who was already in the form of God could empty Himself by adding the form of a servant. And the name above every name given to Him is the name of the Lord, the divine name, given to one who always had a right to it. The emptying is addition of humanity, not loss of deity. This passage is also the seedbed of the kenosis question discussed below.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Chalcedonian Orthodoxy (the faith of the church)
biblicalEvidence.summary: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. For by Him all things were created, and in Him all things hold together. In Him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arians made firstborn of all creation their charter, the Son as the first thing made. Orthodoxy answers from the very next lines. By Him all things were created, so He cannot be among the created things He made. And firstborn here means heir and ruler over creation, the firstborn's rank, not first in a line of creatures. The fullness of God dwelling in Him seals it against any lesser being.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Chalcedonian Orthodoxy (the faith of the church)
biblicalEvidence.summary: The Son is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of His nature, and He upholds the universe by the word of His power. To the Son God says, Your throne, O God, is forever, and let all God's angels worship Him.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arians placed the Son among the angels as their chief. Hebrews 1 was written to crush exactly that. It devotes its whole length to showing the Son is far above the angels, addressed as God, worshiped by the angels, the exact imprint of God's own nature. Orthodoxy reads this as a direct refusal to put the Son anywhere on the creature side of the line.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Chalcedonian Orthodoxy (the faith of the church)
biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus said, Before Abraham was, I am. The crowd picked up stones, because they understood Him to take the divine name God spoke to Moses, I AM, and so to claim to be God.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Some read I am here as merely claiming to predate Abraham, which an exalted creature might. Orthodoxy points to the crowd's reaction. They reached for stones to kill Him for blasphemy. That makes sense only if they heard Him claiming the unspeakable name of God from Exodus 3:14. The eternal present tense, I am rather than I was, says He simply is, the mark of God alone.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Concerning that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. Jesus says plainly there is something He does not know.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Chalcedonian Orthodoxy (the faith of the church) at first glance
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Arians made this their hammer. The Son does not know, therefore the Son is not God. Orthodoxy reads it through the two natures. The one person speaks now from His human nature, which is genuinely limited, and in His humanity He does not know the hour, while in His divine nature He knows all things. This is not God failing to know. It is the Son, in the real human mind He took up, sharing our genuine human not-knowing. The same person can say both, I and the Father are one, and, the Father is greater than I, because He speaks now as God and now as man.

biblicalEvidence.summary: And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man. He grew. He learned. He developed like a real child.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: If you deny Jesus a human mind, as Apollinaris did, you cannot explain how He increased in wisdom. The divine Word does not grow in wisdom. If you deny Him a real body, as the Docetists did, you cannot explain how He grew in stature. Orthodoxy welcomes this verse as proof of a complete and real humanity that genuinely developed, a true human mind learning and a true human body growing. The divine nature remained full and unchanging throughout.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Chalcedonian Orthodoxy (the faith of the church)
biblicalEvidence.summary: Thomas, seeing the risen and wounded Jesus, answered Him, My Lord and my God. And Jesus received it rather than correcting it.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: An Arian must explain why Jesus accepts being called God outright, worship He would have refused if He were a creature. A Nestorian must explain how Thomas addresses the one person, the wounded man standing in front of him, as both Lord and God, with no splitting into a human son he can touch and a divine son he cannot. Orthodoxy reads it as the goal of John's whole Gospel, the single risen person confessed as fully God.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Chalcedonian Orthodoxy (the faith of the church)
biblicalEvidence.summary: Since the children share in flesh and blood, He Himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death He might destroy the devil. He had to be made like His brothers in every respect, to become a merciful and faithful high priest.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Docetists must reckon with He partook of flesh and blood, real shared humanity unto death. Apollinarians must reckon with made like His brothers in every respect, which leaves out no part of human nature, mind included. Orthodoxy reads this as Scripture's own argument for why the full humanity is not optional. The Savior had to take all of what we are to rescue all of what we are.

weighing:
On this doctrine I do not offer you my private opinion, and I want you to feel the difference from how I write about other questions. Here the church has spoken. I am only handing you what was settled long before any of us drew breath. Chalcedon is not one option on a menu. It is the faith. One person, two natures, fully God and fully man, the natures unconfused, unchanged, undivided, and unseparated. I affirm it plainly. And I ask you to receive it as the bedrock it is.

I do not affirm it because a council declared it and I am bound to obey men. I affirm it because every other path the early church walked turned out to cost them the Savior. Make Him less than God and He cannot reach down far enough to save. Make Him less than man and He cannot reach across far enough to stand in your place. Split Him into two persons and it is not God who died for you. Blend His natures into one and He is neither truly God nor truly your brother. Athanasius, Cyril, and the fathers at Nicaea and Chalcedon were not splitting hairs. They were guarding the gospel itself. The words they chose still hold the line.

What remains open even here remains open because the church did not close every question. Only the central one. There are real debates among fully orthodox Christians who all confess Chalcedon, and you should not mistake them for the heresies above. The first is the kenosis debate. Kenosis is a Greek word meaning self-emptying, taken from Philippians 2 where Christ emptied Himself. All the orthodox agree He emptied Himself. They differ on what that emptying means. The older and safer reading is that He emptied Himself not by subtracting any of His deity but by adding humanity and veiling His glory, choosing not to use His divine powers except as the Father willed. Some modern theologians have pressed a stronger view. The Son, they say, somehow set aside the use of certain divine attributes during His earthly life. Hold the gentler version. The stronger versions, pushed too hard, can drift toward the very Arianism Chalcedon ruled out, and careful voices like Stephen Wellum and Donald Macleod have warned against them. But the question of how to read the emptying is a fair one. It is family business, not heresy.

The second open question is the communicatio idiomatum, a Latin phrase meaning the communication of attributes, the rule for how we speak about the one person who has two natures. Because Jesus is one person, what is true of either nature can be said of the person. So we can say God was born and God died, since the person who was born and died is God, even though dying belongs to His humanity, not His deity. All the orthodox agree on that much. Lutherans and the Reformed then divide on how far it goes. Lutherans, to defend Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper, hold that the human nature itself received certain divine attributes. So Christ's humanity can be present everywhere. The Reformed answer with the extra Calvinisticum, a Latin nickname meaning the Calvinist beyond or extra, the teaching that even while fully united to the flesh, the eternal Son also continued to fill and uphold the whole universe beyond the body of Jesus, since the infinite God cannot be contained in a finite body. The Lutheran fears a Christ divided. The Reformed fears a humanity turned into something no longer human. Both confess one person in two natures. They disagree on the plumbing, not the house.
charitableDisagreement:
Let me draw the line carefully, because charity here means different things in different places. Toward the ancient heresies I am firm but not mocking. The Docetist, the Arian, the Apollinarian, the Nestorian, and the Eutychian were almost all trying to protect something true, the holiness of God, the oneness of Christ, the distinction of the natures, and they fell off the road while reaching for it. I will not sneer at people who lost their way trying to honor the Lord. But I will not pretend they kept the faith, because they did not, and the church was right to say so. A different Jesus is a different gospel, and love for a new believer means telling you the truth about that, not blurring it to seem kind.

Toward my orthodox brothers who differ on the kenosis or who stand on the Lutheran or the Reformed side of the communicatio, I extend a wholly different warmth, because we are inside the same house confessing the same Christ. So is this a hill to die on? The two questions left open among the orthodox, how to read the emptying and how far the attributes communicate, are not hills to die on. They are rooms to study in, with brothers you can take communion beside. But the central confession, that Jesus is one person, fully God and fully man, true God of true God, born of the virgin and crucified and risen, is the hill itself. It is the ground the whole church stands on. On that one, yes, men have died, and rightly, because if you lose this Jesus you have lost the only Savior there is.

relatedDebates.note: What does it mean that Christ emptied Himself in Philippians 2? The historic view is that He emptied Himself by addition, taking the form of a servant and veiling His glory while never ceasing to be fully God, and choosing not to draw on His divine powers apart from the Father's will. Some modern kenotic theologians argue the Son actually laid aside the use, or even the possession, of certain divine attributes during His earthly life. The goal was a genuinely human existence. Critics like Stephen Wellum and Donald Macleod warn that the stronger forms make the divine nature changeable and edge toward the creaturely Son that Nicaea condemned. This is a real intramural debate, not a heresy. But the safer ground is the older reading.

relatedDebates.topic: The communicatio idiomatum, Lutheran versus Reformed
relatedDebates.note: All the orthodox agree that because Christ is one person, what is true of either nature can be predicated of the person. So we rightly say God died for us. Lutherans go further and teach that in the union the human nature itself came to share certain divine properties, including a kind of omnipresence, which undergirds their belief in Christ's bodily presence in the Lord's Supper. The Reformed reply with the extra Calvinisticum, that the Son remained fully God beyond the limits of His human body, upholding the universe even while in the womb and on the cross, since the infinite cannot be poured without remainder into the finite. Both sides confess Chalcedon. They divide on whether attributes pass to the nature or only to the person.

Could Jesus have sinned? All the orthodox agree He did not sin (Hebrews 4:15). They divide on whether He could have. Those who hold impeccability, that He was not able to sin, argue that since He is one divine person and God cannot sin, the person who is the Son could not sin even in His human nature. Those who hold peccability, that He was able to sin but freely did not, argue that His temptations were real, and a temptation that has no possibility of success is not a true temptation like ours. Defenders of impeccability answer that the temptations were genuine assaults genuinely resisted in His human nature. The outcome was secured by who He is. This too is a family debate among those who confess the one person in two natures.
